title: Ridge Trails
statement: A topographic survey stores elevations in a grid of equal-length rows. A ridge trail moves between cells that share an edge (up, down, left or right) and must climb strictly at every step. Return the number of cells on the longest ridge trail. A single cell is a trail of length 1.

hints.content: A trail can start anywhere, so think about the longest trail starting at each cell.
longest(cell) = 1 + the maximum of longest(neighbor) over neighbors that are strictly higher.
Because steps strictly climb, a trail can never revisit a cell, so there are no cycles to worry about.
Many trails pass through the same cell, so cache longest(cell) the first time you compute it.
Alternatively, process cells from lowest to highest so every lower neighbor's answer is ready (a topological order). Either way, each cell is solved once.

testCases.explanation: Flat ground: no step climbs strictly.
A single row climbing left to right.
A spiral that climbs through all nine cells.
A 50 × 50 serpentine that climbs through all 2500 cells; exploring every path without memoization cannot finish.

solutions.title: Depth-first search from every cell without caching
solutions.intuition: Explore every climbing trail and keep the longest.
solutions.approach: walk(r, c) returns 1 plus the best walk among strictly higher neighbors. Take the maximum over all starting cells.
solutions.pseudocode:
walk(r, c) = 1 + max(walk(n) for higher neighbors n, default 0)
return max over cells of walk(cell)
commonMistakes: Allowing equal heights, which creates cycles and infinite recursion.
Starting only from the lowest cell; the longest trail may start elsewhere.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Plain DFS explores every climbing trail. Trails overlap heavily, so the same cell's answer is recomputed many times and the cost blows up.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.content: From the cell with 1 at (2,1): climb to 2, then 6, then 9, a length of 4.

solutions.title: Memoized depth-first search
solutions.intuition: The longest climb starting at a cell is fixed, so compute it once and reuse it.
solutions.approach: Keep a memo grid of zeros. walk(r, c) returns the memo if set; otherwise computes 1 + the best higher neighbor and stores it. Return the maximum over all cells.
commonMistakes: Using a visited set instead of a memo; strict climbing already prevents cycles, and visited would wrongly block reuse.
Assuming recursion depth is small; a serpentine grid recurses once per cell, so very large grids would need an iterative order.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Strictly increasing steps make the graph a DAG, so the longest path from each cell is well defined and can be memoized. Every cell is solved once and checks four neighbors, O(rows × cols). For huge grids I'd avoid deep recursion by sorting cells by height and filling the table from low to high, which is a topological order.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.content: walk(2,1) for height 1 → walk(2,0) for 2 → walk(1,0) for 6 → walk(0,0) for 9, which is 1.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: Unwinding: 2, 3, 4. Later cells reuse those memo entries. The answer is 4.
